lesson.title: Like Dissolves Like: A Rule of Thumb Built on Intermolecular Forces
lesson.summary: Like dissolves like is the rule of thumb that polar and ionic solutes dissolve best in polar solvents while nonpolar solutes dissolve best in nonpolar solvents, because dissolving only proceeds when new solute-solvent attractions can replace the ones being broken.
lesson.body:
"Like dissolves like" is the rule of thumb chemists use to predict solubility before running any experiment, and it follows directly from molecular polarity and the solubility limits just described. Polar and ionic solutes tend to dissolve well in polar solvents; nonpolar solutes tend to dissolve well in nonpolar solvents. The reason is the same energetic balance from the last chapter: dissolving only proceeds favorably when the new solute-solvent attractions formed are comparable in strength to the solute-solute and solvent-solvent attractions being broken.

Water is polar and an exceptional hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, which lets it surround and stabilize ions through ion-dipole forces, each ion gets wrapped in a shell of water molecules with the appropriate partial charge facing in, and lets it hydrogen bond directly to other polar molecules like sugars and alcohols. Nonpolar solvents, like hexane, have no such strong local charges to offer; they interact only through weak London dispersion forces, which is exactly the kind of attraction nonpolar solutes like oils and greases also rely on, so the match works well in the other direction.

A mismatch fails for the same reason. Mix oil and water and the water molecules keep their strong mutual hydrogen bonds intact, effectively squeezing the oil out rather than making room for it, because oil can only offer weak dispersion forces in return, nowhere near enough to compete with hydrogen bonding. That is why the two separate into layers instead of blending.

The numbers make the contrast obvious. Ionic, polar NaCl dissolves in water up to about 36 g per 100 g of water, as covered in the last chapter. Nonpolar vegetable oil, by contrast, dissolves in water at less than about 0.1 g per 100 g, so little that it is considered essentially insoluble, a difference of well over three hundredfold between a well matched pairing and a mismatched one.

The rule is a heuristic, not an absolute law, and molecules with mixed character show why. Ethanol has both a polar hydroxyl group, which hydrogen bonds readily with water, and a nonpolar carbon chain, which prefers nonpolar company. That dual personality is exactly why ethanol is miscible with water in every proportion and also dissolves reasonably well in some nonpolar solvents: it is never a perfect match for either, but it is a workable match for both.
